text:
**For most people, LiFePO4 (LFP) is the better choice.** Nearly every source I found says so, and NMC is mostly found in older or small models now.

| | LiFePO4 | NMC |
|---|---|---|
| Cycle life | Roughly 2,000-6,000 cycles to 70-85% | Roughly 500-2,000, depending on the source |
| Heat and safety | More thermally stable and less prone to thermal runaway | Less stable |
| Weight | A bit heavier per Wh | Lighter at the cell level |
| Price per Wh | Median about $0.55 | Median about $0.95 |

**Cycle life** is the biggest difference. At one full cycle a day, a 3,000-cycle LiFePO4 unit lasts about 8 years, while a 500-cycle NMC unit lasts under 2 ([Unplugged Watts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). If you only use it for occasional outages or a few weekends a year, cycle count matters much less, because age and storage conditions become the limit.

**Weight** is NMC's real advantage, but it shrinks in finished products. The cells themselves differ a lot, but the case, inverter and fans weigh the same either way. One database found NMC models only about 10% more energy-dense per pound than LFP ones, and in same-maker pairs the LFP version was just slightly heavier per kWh ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). Another site put the gap at about 16% ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). Compare actual spec sheets rather than assuming the chemistry decides the weight.

**Safety:** LFP cells don't release oxygen when overheated, so failures are less energetic ([PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/learn/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). Any well-made unit with a good battery management system is reasonably safe, though, and LFP just gives you more margin if you store it somewhere hot or near where you sleep.

**When NMC might still make sense:** only if weight is critical, such as carrying it far on foot, and you'll use it rarely. Even then, many makers now sell LFP versions of their older NMC models, so check for those first.

The cycle ratings vary between sources. Some cite 500 cycles for NMC and others 1,000-2,000, and brands don't all measure ratings the same way. Check that a rating states its end point (such as "to 80%"), since a "to 70%" claim is weaker.

**If you want an LFP example for home backup:** the [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2) is a 2,073.6 Wh LiFePO4 station with a 2,600 W inverter and a 6,000+ cycle rating (to 80%). It's listed at $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF, which the source says it tested in BLUETTI's cart today. It isn't expandable, weighs 24.2 kg, and has a 5-year warranty. It's a fit for running a fridge, router and lights for a day or two. Details are on [Dealectric's page](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-elite-200-v2).
